Sets

Union and intersection

A∪B={x:x∈A∨x∈B}A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \lor x \in B\}A∪B={x:x∈A∨x∈B}A∩B={x:x∈A∧x∈B}A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \land x \in B\}A∩B={x:x∈A∧x∈B}

Symbols: ∈\in∈: “belongs to”, ∨\lor∨: or, ∧\land∧: and.

The idea

The union collects everything in AAA or in BBB (or both); the intersection keeps only what is in both. “Or” is inclusive in mathematics, so the common elements belong to the union — but count each element once.

Worked example

A={1,2,3,4}A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}A={1,2,3,4}, B={3,4,5}B = \{3, 4, 5\}B={3,4,5}: A∪B={1,2,3,4,5}A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}A∪B={1,2,3,4,5} and A∩B={3,4}A \cap B = \{3, 4\}A∩B={3,4}.

Complement and difference

Aˉ=U∖A\bar A = U \setminus AAˉ=U∖AA∖B=A∩BˉA \setminus B = A \cap \bar BA∖B=A∩Bˉ

Symbols: UUU: the universal set (everything under study); ∖\setminus∖: “minus”, remove the elements.

The idea

The complement Aˉ\bar AAˉ is everything in the universe UUU that is not in AAA. The difference A∖BA \setminus BA∖B removes from AAA whatever is also in BBB — the same as A∩BˉA \cap \bar BA∩Bˉ. Order matters: A∖B≠B∖AA \setminus B \ne B \setminus AA∖B=B∖A.

Worked example

U={1,…,10}U = \{1, \dots, 10\}U={1,…,10}, AAA = even numbers: Aˉ={1,3,5,7,9}\bar A = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9\}Aˉ={1,3,5,7,9}. With B={1,2,3}B = \{1, 2, 3\}B={1,2,3}: A∖B={4,6,8,10}A \setminus B = \{4, 6, 8, 10\}A∖B={4,6,8,10}.

De Morgan’s laws

A∪B‾=Aˉ∩Bˉ\overline{A \cup B} = \bar A \cap \bar BA∪B=Aˉ∩BˉA∩B‾=Aˉ∪Bˉ\overline{A \cap B} = \bar A \cup \bar BA∩B=Aˉ∪Bˉ

The idea

“Not in (AAA or BBB)” means outside both circles: not in AAA and not in BBB. Complementing swaps ∪\cup∪ and ∩\cap∩. The shaded region outside both circles is A∪B‾=Aˉ∩Bˉ\overline{A \cup B} = \bar A \cap \bar BA∪B=Aˉ∩Bˉ.

Worked example

Students who play neither football nor tennis = not football AND not tennis. Students who do not play both = not football OR not tennis.

Distributive laws

A∩(B∪C)=(A∩B)∪(A∩C)A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)A∩(B∪C)=(A∩B)∪(A∩C)A∪(B∩C)=(A∪B)∩(A∪C)A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)A∪(B∩C)=(A∪B)∩(A∪C)

The idea

∩\cap∩ distributes over ∪\cup∪ like multiplication over addition — and, unlike numbers, ∪\cup∪ also distributes over ∩\cap∩. Check with a three-circle diagram: both sides shade the same region.

Worked example

A={1,2,3}A = \{1, 2, 3\}A={1,2,3}, B={2,4}B = \{2, 4\}B={2,4}, C={3,4}C = \{3, 4\}C={3,4}: B∪C={2,3,4}B \cup C = \{2, 3, 4\}B∪C={2,3,4}, so A∩(B∪C)={2,3}A \cap (B \cup C) = \{2, 3\}A∩(B∪C)={2,3}; and (A∩B)∪(A∩C)={2}∪{3}(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C) = \{2\} \cup \{3\}(A∩B)∪(A∩C)={2}∪{3} — the same.

Subsets

A⊆B  ⟺  A∩B=A  ⟺  A∪B=BA \subseteq B \iff A \cap B = A \iff A \cup B = BA⊆B⟺A∩B=A⟺A∪B=B

A set with nnn elements has 2n2^n2n subsets (2n−12^n - 12n−1 proper, 2n−22^n - 22n−2 proper non-empty).

Symbols: ⊆\subseteq⊆: “is contained in” (every element of AAA is in BBB).

The idea

A⊆BA \subseteq BA⊆B means every element of AAA is in BBB: the circle AAA sits inside BBB. Then intersecting with BBB changes nothing in AAA, and adding AAA to BBB changes nothing in BBB. A set with nnn elements has 2n2^n2n subsets (each element in or out).

Worked example

{a,b,c}\{a, b, c\}{a,b,c} has 23=82^3 = 823=8 subsets: ∅\varnothing∅, {a}\{a\}{a}, {b}\{b\}{b}, {c}\{c\}{c}, {a,b}\{a, b\}{a,b}, {a,c}\{a, c\}{a,c}, {b,c}\{b, c\}{b,c}, {a,b,c}\{a, b, c\}{a,b,c}.

Counting

∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣

The idea

Counting AAA and then BBB counts the common part twice, so subtract it once. Knowing any three of ∣A∣\lvert A\rvert∣A∣, ∣B∣\lvert B\rvert∣B∣, ∣A∩B∣\lvert A \cap B\rvert∣A∩B∣, ∣A∪B∣\lvert A \cup B\rvert∣A∪B∣ gives the fourth.

Worked example

In a class, 20 study French, 15 study German and 7 study both: 20+15−7=2820 + 15 - 7 = 2820+15−7=28 study at least one.

Number sets

N⊂Z⊂Q⊂R⊂C\mathbb N \subset \mathbb Z \subset \mathbb Q \subset \mathbb R \subset \mathbb CN⊂Z⊂Q⊂R⊂C

Symbols: N\mathbb NN natural, Z\mathbb ZZ integer, Q\mathbb QQ rational, R\mathbb RR real, C\mathbb CC complex numbers.

The idea

Each set extends the previous one to allow a new operation: Z\mathbb ZZ adds negatives (subtraction), Q\mathbb QQ fractions (division), R\mathbb RR limits like 2\sqrt22​ and π\piπ, C\mathbb CC square roots of negatives. Classify a number by its simplest form: 9=3\sqrt9 = 39​=3 is a natural number.

Worked example

−3∈Z∖N-3 \in \mathbb Z \setminus \mathbb N−3∈Z∖N; 25∈Q∖Z\tfrac25 \in \mathbb Q \setminus \mathbb Z52​∈Q∖Z; 2,π∈R∖Q\sqrt2, \pi \in \mathbb R \setminus \mathbb Q2​,π∈R∖Q (irrational); −1=i∈C∖R\sqrt{-1} = i \in \mathbb C \setminus \mathbb R−1​=i∈C∖R.

Intervals

[a,b]={a≤x≤b}[a, b] = \{a \le x \le b\}[a,b]={a≤x≤b}(a,b)={a<x<b}(a, b) = \{a < x < b\}(a,b)={a<x<b}[a,∞)={x≥a}[a, \infty) = \{x \ge a\}[a,∞)={x≥a}

The idea

An interval is a piece of the number line. A square bracket includes the endpoint (filled dot), a round one excludes it (hollow dot); ∞\infty∞ always gets a round bracket. Intersections of intervals are the overlap.

Worked example

[−1,3)∩(0,5]=(0,3)[-1, 3) \cap (0, 5] = (0, 3)[−1,3)∩(0,5]=(0,3): the overlap starts after 0 (excluded by the second) and stops before 3 (excluded by the first).

Negations

¬(p∧q)≡¬p∨¬q\lnot(p \land q) \equiv \lnot p \lor \lnot q¬(p∧q)≡¬p∨¬q¬(p∨q)≡¬p∧¬q\lnot(p \lor q) \equiv \lnot p \land \lnot q¬(p∨q)≡¬p∧¬q

Symbols: ¬\lnot¬: not, ∧\land∧: and, ∨\lor∨: or, ≡\equiv≡: “is equivalent to”.

The idea

To deny “ppp and qqq” it is enough that one of them fails: ¬p∨¬q\lnot p \lor \lnot q¬p∨¬q. To deny “ppp or qqq” both must fail: ¬p∧¬q\lnot p \land \lnot q¬p∧¬q. Negation swaps ∧\land∧ and ∨\lor∨ — De Morgan again.

Worked example

“It is not true that it is sunny and warm” = “it is not sunny or it is not warm”. “x<0x < 0x<0 or x>5x > 5x>5” is negated as “x≥0x \ge 0x≥0 and x≤5x \le 5x≤5”, i.e. 0≤x≤50 \le x \le 50≤x≤5.

Implication

p⇒q ≡ ¬p∨qp \Rightarrow q \ \equiv\ \lnot p \lor qp⇒q ≡ ¬p∨q¬(p⇒q)≡p∧¬q\lnot(p \Rightarrow q) \equiv p \land \lnot q¬(p⇒q)≡p∧¬q

Symbols: p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q: “if ppp then qqq”; it is false only when ppp is true and qqq false.

The idea

“If ppp then qqq” only fails when ppp happens and qqq does not. So it means the same as “not ppp, or qqq”, and its negation is “ppp and not qqq” — a counterexample. The negation of an implication is never another implication.

Worked example

“If nnn is prime, then nnn is odd” is false because of n=2n = 2n=2: prime and not odd — exactly p∧¬qp \land \lnot qp∧¬q.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Converse, inverse, contrapositive

q⇒pq \Rightarrow pq⇒p¬p⇒¬q\lnot p \Rightarrow \lnot q¬p⇒¬q¬q⇒¬p\lnot q \Rightarrow \lnot p¬q⇒¬p

Only the contrapositive (the third) is always equivalent to p ⇒ q.

The idea

From p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q you can build three statements. The contrapositive ¬q⇒¬p\lnot q \Rightarrow \lnot p¬q⇒¬p always has the same truth value as the original. The converse q⇒pq \Rightarrow pq⇒p and the inverse ¬p⇒¬q\lnot p \Rightarrow \lnot q¬p⇒¬q agree with each other, but not necessarily with the original.

Worked example

“If it rains, the street is wet” (true). Contrapositive: “if the street is dry, it is not raining” (true). Converse: “if the street is wet, it rains” (false — someone may have washed it).

Necessary and sufficient

Sufficient condition

p⇒q:  p→q ✓p \Rightarrow q:\ \ p \to q \ \checkmarkp⇒q:  p→q ✓

If p ⇒ q, then p is sufficient for q and q is necessary for p.

The idea

If p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q, then knowing ppp is enough to guarantee qqq: ppp is sufficient for qqq. And qqq is necessary for ppp: without qqq, ppp cannot happen. The arrow points from the sufficient condition to the necessary one.

Worked example

x=3⇒x2=9x = 3 \Rightarrow x^2 = 9x=3⇒x2=9: being 3 is sufficient for having square 9, but not necessary (−3-3−3 also works). Having square 9 is necessary for being 3.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

With sets

P={x:p(x)}, Q={x:q(x)}:P = \{x : p(x)\},\ Q = \{x : q(x)\}:P={x:p(x)}, Q={x:q(x)}:p⇒q  ⟺  P⊆Qp \Rightarrow q \iff P \subseteq Qp⇒q⟺P⊆Q

The smaller set is the sufficient condition, the bigger one the necessary condition.

The idea

Let PPP and QQQ be the sets of values where ppp and qqq are true. “p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q” says every point of PPP is in QQQ: P⊆QP \subseteq QP⊆Q. The smaller set gives the sufficient condition, the larger the necessary one.

Worked example

ppp: 1<x<21 < x < 21<x<2, qqq: 0<x<30 < x < 30<x<3. Since (1,2)⊆(0,3)(1, 2) \subseteq (0, 3)(1,2)⊆(0,3) (pink inside yellow), p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q: ppp is sufficient, qqq is necessary.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Necessary and sufficient

p  ⟺  q  ⟺  P=Qp \iff q \iff P = Qp⟺q⟺P=Q

The idea

When the implication goes both ways, ppp and qqq are true for exactly the same values: P=QP = QP=Q. Then each can replace the other — that is what “if and only if” means, and what solving an equation by equivalent steps relies on.

Worked example

x2=4  ⟺  x=2∨x=−2x^2 = 4 \iff x = 2 \lor x = -2x2=4⟺x=2∨x=−2. But x=2x = 2x=2 alone is only sufficient: the step “x2=4x^2 = 4x2=4, so x=2x = 2x=2” loses a solution.

Quantifiers

For all, there exists

∀x∈A: p(x)\forall x \in A:\ p(x)∀x∈A: p(x)∃ x∈A: p(x)\exists\,x \in A:\ p(x)∃x∈A: p(x)

Symbols: ∀\forall∀: “for all”, ∃\exists∃: “there exists (at least one)”.

The idea

“∀x\forall x∀x” claims something for every xxx of the set — one failure makes it false. “∃ x\exists\,x∃x” claims at least one xxx works — one example makes it true. The set matters: ∃ x:x2=2\exists\,x: x^2 = 2∃x:x2=2 is true in R\mathbb RR but false in Q\mathbb QQ.

Worked example

“∀n∈N\forall n \in \mathbb N∀n∈N: n2≥nn^2 \ge nn2≥n” is true. “∀x∈R\forall x \in \mathbb R∀x∈R: x2≥xx^2 \ge xx2≥x” is false: x=12x = \tfrac12x=21​ gives 14<12\tfrac14 < \tfrac1241​<21​.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Negating quantifiers

¬(∀x: p(x))≡∃ x: ¬p(x)\lnot\big(\forall x:\ p(x)\big) \equiv \exists\,x:\ \lnot p(x)¬(∀x: p(x))≡∃x: ¬p(x)¬(∃ x: p(x))≡∀x: ¬p(x)\lnot\big(\exists\,x:\ p(x)\big) \equiv \forall x:\ \lnot p(x)¬(∃x: p(x))≡∀x: ¬p(x)

Example: the negation of “∀x, x2≥0\forall x,\ x^2 \ge 0∀x, x2≥0” is “∃ x, x2<0\exists\,x,\ x^2 < 0∃x, x2<0”.

The idea

“Not every xxx works” means some xxx fails; “no xxx works” means every xxx fails. Negating swaps ∀\forall∀ and ∃\exists∃ and negates the property — keep the set the same.

Worked example

Negate “every student passed”: “some student did not pass” (not “no student passed”). Negate “∃ x∈R\exists\,x \in \mathbb R∃x∈R: x2<0x^2 < 0x2<0”: “∀x∈R\forall x \in \mathbb R∀x∈R: x2≥0x^2 \ge 0x2≥0”.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Unique existence

∃! x: p(x)\exists!\,x:\ p(x)∃!x: p(x)

Symbols: ∃!\exists!∃!: “there exists exactly one”.

The idea

“∃! x\exists!\,x∃!x” says two things: there is an xxx (existence) and there are no two different ones (uniqueness). To prove uniqueness, suppose x1x_1x1​ and x2x_2x2​ both work and show x1=x2x_1 = x_2x1​=x2​.

Worked example

2x+1=72x + 1 = 72x+1=7 has the unique solution x=3x = 3x=3: if 2x1+1=2x2+12x_1 + 1 = 2x_2 + 12x1​+1=2x2​+1 then x1=x2x_1 = x_2x1​=x2​. But x2=9x^2 = 9x2=9 has two, so “∃! x\exists!\,x∃!x: x2=9x^2 = 9x2=9” is false.

Methods of proof

Mathematical induction

P(1) ∧ (P(k)⇒P(k+1)) ⇒ ∀n≥1: P(n)P(1) \ \land\ \big(P(k) \Rightarrow P(k + 1)\big) \ \Rightarrow\ \forall n \ge 1:\ P(n)P(1) ∧ (P(k)⇒P(k+1)) ⇒ ∀n≥1: P(n)

Base case, then assume P(k)P(k)P(k) and prove P(k+1)P(k + 1)P(k+1).

Symbols: P(n)P(n)P(n): the statement for the number nnn.

The idea

Like dominoes: show the first one falls (P(1)P(1)P(1)), and that each falling domino knocks over the next (P(k)⇒P(k+1)P(k) \Rightarrow P(k + 1)P(k)⇒P(k+1)). Then all fall. In the step you may use P(k)P(k)P(k) — that is the whole point.

Worked example

1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)21 + 2 + \dots + n = \tfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}1+2+⋯+n=2n(n+1)​. Base: 1=1⋅221 = \tfrac{1\cdot 2}{2}1=21⋅2​. Step: k(k+1)2+(k+1)=(k+1)(k+2)2\tfrac{k(k + 1)}{2} + (k + 1) = \tfrac{(k + 1)(k + 2)}{2}2k(k+1)​+(k+1)=2(k+1)(k+2)​ — the formula for k+1k + 1k+1.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Contradiction

¬p⇒⊥  ∴ p\lnot p \Rightarrow \bot \ \ \therefore\ p¬p⇒⊥  ∴ p

Classic: 2\sqrt22​ is irrational; there are infinitely many primes.

Symbols: ⊥\bot⊥: a contradiction (something false), ∴\therefore∴: “therefore”.

The idea

Assume the opposite of what you want to prove and reason until you reach something impossible (⊥\bot⊥). Since correct reasoning cannot lead from a truth to an impossibility, the assumption was false — so the statement is true.

Worked example

2\sqrt22​ is irrational. Suppose 2=ab\sqrt2 = \tfrac ab2​=ba​ in lowest terms. Then a2=2b2a^2 = 2b^2a2=2b2, so aaa is even, a=2ka = 2ka=2k; then b2=2k2b^2 = 2k^2b2=2k2, so bbb is even too — but the fraction was in lowest terms. Contradiction.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Contrapositive

¬q⇒¬p  ∴ p⇒q\lnot q \Rightarrow \lnot p \ \ \therefore\ p \Rightarrow q¬q⇒¬p  ∴ p⇒q

The idea

Instead of p⇒qp \Rightarrow qp⇒q, prove the equivalent ¬q⇒¬p\lnot q \Rightarrow \lnot p¬q⇒¬p. It helps when “not qqq” gives you something concrete to work with — e.g. “nnn odd” gives n=2k+1n = 2k + 1n=2k+1.

Worked example

“If n2n^2n2 is even then nnn is even.” Contrapositive: if nnn is odd, n=2k+1n = 2k + 1n=2k+1, then n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1n^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1n2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1 is odd. Done.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Counterexample

∃ x: ¬p(x) ⇒ ¬(∀x: p(x))\exists\,x:\ \lnot p(x) \ \Rightarrow\ \lnot\big(\forall x:\ p(x)\big)∃x: ¬p(x) ⇒ ¬(∀x: p(x))

One counterexample is enough to disprove a “for all” statement.

The idea

A “for all” statement is destroyed by a single case where it fails. No number of examples can prove it, but one counterexample disproves it. Look at small, extreme or special values first.

Worked example

“n2+n+41n^2 + n + 41n2+n+41 is prime for every nnn” holds for n=0,…,39n = 0, \dots, 39n=0,…,39, yet n=40n = 40n=40 gives 1681=4121681 = 41^21681=412. Forty examples did not prove it; one value disproved it.
